question: Reports in the press indicate that Antonio Angelucci MP wants to buy the AGI news agency (Agenzia Giornalistica Italia), adding another outlet to the three Italian newspapers (Libero, Il Giornale e Il Tempo) he already owns. Acquired by ENI in 1965, AGI is Italy’s second-biggest news agency, has offices in 15 of the country’s regional capitals (as well as one in Brussels) and broadcasts news in six languages.

AGI’s news staff have recently aired their serious concerns that the potential takeover – which has never been officially denied – could jeopardise their editorial independence. The newsroom will stage a five-day walkout unless management promptly sheds some light on the agency's future. In the light of the above: 1.
Is the Commission aware of the potential takeover of AGI?
Given the adoption of the Media Freedom Act, what measures will the Commission take if AGI’s editorial independence is compromised?
answer: Subject: Press freedom at risk in Italy Media ownership in Italy is converging into the hands of fewer and fewer people. Lega MP Antonio Angelucci is in talks with ENI about buying Italian news agency AGI, in which the Ministry of Finance — headed by fellow Lega member Giancarlo Giorgetti — has a stake. Alongside his parliamentary duties, Angelucci already owns three dailies: Libero, Il Giornale and Il Tempo.

If he were to acquire AGI too, he would gain an even more dominant position in the Italian publishing market. Let us not forget that, in addition to Angelucci, an MP from a political party in power, the Berlusconi family, which funds Forza Italia, owns Mediaset.

What is more, Matteo Renzi’s act reforming governance at the public broadcaster, Rai, is still in force; this empowers the government to appoint directors and other senior managers at the company. In the light of the above: 1.
In the Commission’s view, would this further acquisition be in line with the recently adopted Media Freedom Act?
Will it ask Italy to provide an explanation for the concentration of its media in the hands of a few owners and to justify their political connections?

Joint answer given by Vice-President Jourová on behalf of the European Commission (5 June 2024) The Commission is aware of the discussions on the potential takeover referred to by the Honourable Members. The Commission is following developments on media freedom and media pluralism, in particular in the context of the annual rule of law report (1).

The Commission acted to regulate the provision of media services in the internal market and strengthen media pluralism and editorial independence, with the European Media Freedom Act (EMFA (2)). It entered into force in May 2024 and will apply from August 2025.

The EMFA will require that media service providers offering news and current affairs content take measures guaranteeing that editorial decisions can be taken freely within the established editorial line. In this respect, the Commission Recommendation (3) puts forward a set of measures for media service providers to consider in order to guarantee the independent process of news content production.

The EMFA also requires Member States to ensure that media market concentrations, which could significantly impact media pluralism and editorial independence, are subject to an independent assessment based on objective, non-discriminatory and proportionate criteria set out at national level.

Safeguards for editorial independence, including the measures taken by media service providers to guarantee the independence of editorial decisions, are among the elements that national regulatory authorities or bodies have to take into account when assessing media market concentrations.

The EMFA provides a mechanism for the European Board for Media Services and the Commission to issue opinions on concentrations likely to affect the internal market’s functioning. The Commission will monitor and ensure the respect of the EMFA and its implementation by Member States.
